name: Tara Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a loader underground at Kestrel Hill, a gold mine about half an hour from home. The proper name is an LHD, load-haul-dump, which is basically a low, long bucket loader built to fit in the tunnels. I muck out the rock after they fire the blasts and tram it to the ore pass, back and forth, ten or eleven hours, with my headlamp and the radio for company.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Just over a year. Before that I did twelve years in aged care, nights mostly, and my back and my bank account both gave up on it. My partner Ben's a plumber, and when a friend of his said the mine was taking on women and paying well, I went for it. We've got two kids, Ruby's fourteen and Sam's ten, and the mine money means we've got nearly a year's worth saved for the first time ever.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work you can see: the drawpoint's full, then it's empty. I'm still not great at it, my trainer Joe says I'm too gentle with the bucket. The hard bit is the dust and the noise, and some mornings you go in in the dark and come out in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because we've got bigger problems underground than robots, like ventilation and fatigue. I'd say that at the toolbox talk and probably on the union group chat. Maybe now they'll spend the money on things that actually keep us safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I get to keep learning this job properly. I'm only a year in, and I'd like to be the one Joe calls when there's a tricky drawpoint, not the new girl. So, honestly, relief with a bit of disappointment that nothing better comes of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. I'd keep putting the extra bit into savings and finish my health and safety rep training through the union, which I started in spring. Maybe book the family trip to the coast we keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Tired, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bit of disappointment. What would you have wanted AI to fix?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a computer could do the shift rosters so nobody ends up on four nights in a row, I'd kiss it. That's the kind of thing I'd want. Instead it'll be writing marketing emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI yourself at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used one to help write my first safety report because I hadn't written anything formal since school. Ruby showed me how. I wouldn't trust it underground, mind.

S0.say: She'd say at the toolbox talk and on the union chat that underground has bigger problems than robots, like ventilation and fatigue. She'd hope the money goes to safety instead.
S0.think: She's relieved she can keep learning the job and stop being the new girl. She's slightly disappointed AI won't fix anything useful, like fair rosters.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving, finishes her union health and safety rep training started in spring, and books the long-postponed family trip to the coast.
S0.feel: Calm, tired, a little let down.
S0.quote: If a computer could do the shift rosters so nobody ends up on four nights in a row, I'd kiss it.
S0.fieldNote: Tara views AI through a safety and fairness lens straight away. She'd have liked it to fix rosters, not marketing. She uses AI occasionally, learned from her daughter, but draws a firm line at trusting it underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs a say in how it's rolled out, especially underground where a machine and a person can meet in a tunnel. I'd say that at the safety committee. Online I'd post about the rules we need before anything driverless goes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, loaders are already half remote at some mines. You sit in a room on the surface with joysticks and screens. I could end up doing my job from a chair with a cup of tea, and I'm not sure that's bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the people who go first say about it. If the remote loader jobs turned out fine, I'd put my hand up for the training in the second or third intake, not the first. Meanwhile I'd keep the savings where they are and push hard as a safety rep for proper rules on mixed traffic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see a way through, but it depends on the company doing it fairly, and I've seen how they treat people when budgets are tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe, my trainer. He's fifty-eight and he's brilliant on a real machine, but he hates screens. I can see them offering him a remote job and him just retiring instead, and losing everything he knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait for the second intake. Why not the first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first lot always gets the bugs. I'm not a pioneer, I'm the second person across the bridge. But I'd be standing at the bridge with my boots on.

S1.say: She'd say the union must have a say in rollout, especially underground where machines and people share tunnels. She'd post online about the safety rules needed first.
S1.think: She knows loaders are already partly remote at some mines and thinks working from a surface chair might not be bad. Her worry is whether the company does it fairly.
S1.do: Watches how the first remote-operator trainees fare and volunteers for the second or third intake, keeps savings untouched, and pushes as a safety rep for rules on mixed traffic.
S1.feel: Uneasy but able to see a way through.
S1.quote: I could end up doing my job from a chair with a cup of tea, and I'm not sure that's bad.
S1.fieldNote: Tara is neither scared nor eager, just watchful. Her description of herself as the second person across the bridge sums up her steady style. Her worry is more for older colleagues like her trainer than for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need governments that plan, and that companies shouldn't be allowed to sack whole crews overnight. I'd go to rallies. I'd say we need a basic income or something like it, fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too quick for anyone to get it right, and when people rush underground, people get hurt. My job would go, and aged care, my old fallback, gets robots too in that picture. I think I'd be fine for money for a year or so, but not for what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, sit down with Ben and work out what we've got: about eleven months of savings, plus his trade, which might last a bit longer. Stop the extension we've been planning on the house. Then I'd be in every union meeting about redundancy terms and writing to my local member about income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Clearly anxious, but not lost. We've got a cushion and we've got each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would two years of warning change things compared to it arriving with none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely. Two years is about one training course. I'd maybe finish my safety rep stuff and use it to get on a transition committee, because at least then I'd know what's coming before the notice goes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruby and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, in small bits. Ruby would ask straight out, she's that kind of kid. I'd tell her Mum went down a mine at forty-two, so Mum can learn something else at forty-four.

S2.say: She'd say this is why governments must plan, that companies shouldn't sack crews overnight, and that something like a basic income is needed quickly.
S2.think: She thinks two years is too fast to do safely, and that both her job and her old aged-care fallback would go. Money would last a year, not longer.
S2.do: Reviews the eleven months of savings with her partner, cancels the planned house extension, attends union redundancy meetings, and writes to her local representative about income support.
S2.feel: Clearly anxious, but steadied by savings and her partner.
S2.quote: I'd tell her Mum went down a mine at forty-two, so Mum can learn something else at forty-four.
S2.fieldNote: Tara's instinct is to get inside the process, joining a transition committee so she knows first. Her fear isn't for money in year one but for what follows. Her line about learning something new at forty-four echoes her late move into mining and is her main source of confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this properly if we start now: training funds, safety rules, notice periods. I'd say it louder at the safety committee than anywhere else. I'd push for a fund paid for by the companies that profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to see who's doing well out of it and copy them. That's my style. I'd let the early movers show the way, then follow quickly, so maybe year two I'd make a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, keep working and saving, and ask HR what training they're planning for remote and maintenance roles. By year two, if the remote jobs look solid, I'd get the ticket. I'd also look at an enrolled nursing course part-time, as a backup, because I know care work and I think people will still want a human hand there for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most days, anxious some nights. Five years is long enough to plan and short enough to keep you awake now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got two backups there: remote operation and nursing. Which one is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly, and that's the point. One's the safe bet and one's the one I'd actually be proud of. Nursing's the proud one. I'd find out which one is still standing by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut, money-wise, to fund a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, we'd manage. Probably the second car. Ben's van does for him, and I'd get the mine bus. And no new phone for me, which Ruby will find more upsetting than I will.

S3.say: She'd say there's time to do this properly with training funds, safety rules and notice periods. She'd push for a training fund paid by the companies that profit.
S3.think: She thinks five years lets her watch the early movers and follow quickly, probably making her own move in year two.
S3.do: Asks HR in year one about remote and maintenance training, gets a remote ticket by year two if the jobs look solid, and starts a part-time enrolled nursing course as a backup, selling the second car to help.
S3.quote: One's the safe bet and one's the one I'd actually be proud of.
S3.fieldNote: Five years suits Tara's steady style: enough time to watch others, then follow. Running two backup plans side by side is very her, one safe and one meaningful. The return of care work as the plan she'd be proud of was a surprise after she'd left it for her back and her bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a disgrace if we waste it. I'd say the companies should be made to fund retraining now, not in year nine. I'd probably post that last bit online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years and I'm fifty-three. I'd be one of the better loader drivers by then, and probably one of the last. I think I'd be all right, but I'd want to leave on my own terms and not get pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep mining for the first few years and keep saving hard. I'd do the nursing course slowly, one unit at a time, over three or four years. And I'd make sure Ruby picks something for uni where a person is the point, not the process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled, with a bit of unease underneath. It feels like something I can get ahead of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't need the safe bet. With five years I'd grab the remote ticket just in case. With ten I'd go straight for the nursing, slowly, and enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Ruby choosing her studies. Have you talked to her about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. She wants to do marine biology, which I love. I'd just tell her to make sure she's the one in the boat, not the one typing up the data.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a gift if used and a disgrace if wasted, and that companies should fund retraining now rather than late.
S4.think: She expects to be fifty-three and among the last loader drivers, and thinks she'd be fine as long as she leaves on her own terms.
S4.do: Keeps mining and saving for the first few years, takes a nursing course one unit at a time over three to four years, and guides her daughter towards studies where a person is the point.
S4.feel: Fairly settled, with mild unease underneath.
S4.quote: I'd just tell her to make sure she's the one in the boat, not the one typing up the data.
S4.fieldNote: The extra time lets Tara drop her safety-net plan and go straight for the work she values. Her concern shifts to her daughter's choices. She remains firmly progressive about who should pay, but personally she sounds almost hopeful here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because of me so much, but because rushing underground gets people hurt, and because everyone loses their backup at once. What would help is a training fund the companies pay into and real notice, at least a year, before any crew is cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety, and that's what I think about most. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, but nobody asks what happens when a robot loader meets a person in a tunnel that's two metres wide.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, but nobody asks what happens when a robot loader meets a person in a tunnel that's two metres wide.
portrait: Tara Evans is a 43-year-old former aged-care worker who now runs an underground loader at a gold mine, a year into the job and still learning. She's married to a plumber, has two kids and almost a year's savings, and is training as a union health and safety rep. She's progressive and steady: she uses AI now and then, waits for others to test new things, then follows quickly. She stays calm to uneasy in most scenarios, becomes anxious only with two-year AGI, and treats nursing as the backup she'd actually be proud of.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because rushing automation underground gets people hurt and everyone loses their backup at once.
whatWouldHelp: A training fund paid for by the companies and at least a year's notice before any crew is cut.
